description:
The eight use-case wrappers (verify_tls_server, verify_tls_client_dns, verify_tls_client_mailbox, verify_smime_signer, verify_smime_recipient, verify_code_signer, verify_time_stamper, verify_ocsp_responder) are concrete free functions with concrete signatures. Each one bakes in:

- Signature verifier: always &DefaultVerifier (hardcoded; PKIX-sqek.9 covers the runtime cost).
- AIA fetcher: always &NoAiaFetcher (hardcoded; PKIX-sqek.4 covers the runtime cost).
- Argument ordering: (chain, anchors, [identity], profile, now_unix, revocation).
- Return type: Result<ValidatedPath, Error>.

Every callsite of `verify_tls_server(chain, anchors, name, profile, now, revocation)` depends on this exact six-argument shape. Adding any new parameter — a fetcher, a logger, a metrics sink, a per-call policy override — is a breaking change to a published signature.

WHY IT MATTERS FOR THE CALLER:

The slash-command checklist's "Public surface immutability" section calls out "Once a function signature, trait method, struct field, enum variant, type alias, or re-export ships in a 0.x.y release, callers depend on it. A breaking change requires a major version bump and caller-side migration."

This is the classic "config struct vs positional args" question. Three credible patterns exist:

(a) **Status quo.** Keep eight concrete functions; accept that future evolution adds parameters as breaking changes. The argument structure is read-at-the-callsite and self-documenting. Cost: every parameter add is a 2.0.

(b) **Single config struct per use case.** `verify_tls_server(config: &TlsServerVerification<'_>)` where the struct is `#[non_exhaustive]` and uses the builder pattern. Adding fields is non-breaking. Cost: callsites lose the positional-arg discipline that makes wrong-order bugs unlikely.

(c) **Builder on the verifier itself.** Make each wrapper a method on `Verifier`: `verifier.verify_tls_server(chain, &name)`. The signature evolution problem then lives on `Verifier` (covered by PKIX-sqek.19, also closely related to PKIX-sqek.4's wrapper-genericity question). This collapses the three filings into one re-shape decision.

(c) is the most natural fit given PKIX-sqek.4 (wrappers should grow generic over A: AiaFetcher = NoAiaFetcher to match Verifier's shape) and PKIX-sqek.19 (Verifier itself wants a builder-shaped construction). The natural endpoint is: Verifier owns the trust state; wrappers are methods; signature evolution lives on Verifier. Eight free functions becomes eight methods + Verifier construction, and parameter adds become non-breaking via #[non_exhaustive] config structs argument types.

The CHANGELOG entry already describes verify_chain as a "thin wrapper around Verifier::verify_one." The use-case wrappers should follow the same model — wrappers as methods, not free functions.

PRE-1.0 FRAMING (AGENTS.md): every wrapper that ships at 1.0 as a free function commits the maintainer to that signature forever. The cost of moving from free-function to method (or to a config struct) is one breaking-change minor bump before 1.0; the cost of doing it after 1.0 is a 2.0 affecting every consumer.

This finding is intentionally a sibling of PKIX-sqek.4 and PKIX-sqek.19 — same root question, different angles. The right resolution is unified.
title: Use-case wrapper signatures (8 concrete fns) are locked: signature evolution requires breaking change or new function
